# Self-Evolving Agentic Workflows via Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks

###### Abstract

Agentic workflows organize complex tasks into reusable procedures.
However, invoking an LLM at every step incurs repeated inference costs
and delays. We propose a framework for self-evolving agentic workflows
through semantic task decomposition. Each subtask has explicit
applicability conditions and a procedure that executes code or invokes a
model as needed. An agent uses execution feedback to refine the
decomposition and update these procedures. Experiments in the GLEE
competition show the framework on bargaining, negotiation and
persuasion. Most observed final-decision procedures are implemented in
code. Code is available at
[Applied-Machine-Learning-Lab/NeurIPS2026_SeaFlow](https://github.com/Applied-Machine-Learning-Lab/NeurIPS2026_SeaFlow).

## 1 Introduction

LLM-based agents use model reasoning to carry out complex tasks. Agentic
workflows organize this process into explicit steps whose connections
determine execution ([Khattab et al., 2024](#bib.bib5); [Zhang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib14)). The resulting procedure can be reused across inputs.
An agent can construct the procedure and revise it using execution
feedback ([Hu et al., 2025](#bib.bib4); [Cheng et al.,
2024](#bib.bib2)).

When every workflow step requires a model call, inference overhead grows
with the number of steps, on top of the reasoning cost within each
call ([Fu et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)). The resulting delay can make a
workflow unsuitable for time-sensitive interactions, while repeated
execution increases its cost. Some of this overhead comes from using
model reasoning for steps that already have defined solutions. Recent
work reduces this dependence by making more of the decision process
directly executable ([Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib11); [Zhang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib13); [Qi et al., 2026](#bib.bib9)). This motivates task
decompositions that specify where agent reasoning is needed and leave
the remaining steps to code.

Our framework begins with (1) semantic task decomposition, through which
an agent organizes decisions into subtasks based on the conditions
observed during interaction. This decomposition provides the basis for
(2) defining a solution procedure for each subtask, so model reasoning
need not be used throughout the workflow. Execution then provides
evidence for (3) revising the workflow. When a subtask handles an
observed situation poorly, the agent changes its scope or solution
procedure. We examine this process across development iterations in
three GLEE environments ([Shapira et al., 2024](#bib.bib10)), using
recorded actions to show how the resulting workflows make decisions.

Our main contributions are as follows:

- •
  We propose a framework for constructing agentic workflows through
  semantic task decomposition. The framework organizes complex
  interactive decisions into a hierarchy of subtasks, with each subtask
  defining when it applies and how it is solved.
- •
  We develop a feedback-driven method for improving these workflows. An
  agent uses execution records and task results to identify problems. It
  then divides subtasks further or changes how they are solved in later
  iterations of the evolving workflow.
- •
  We evaluate the method across three GLEE environments and analyze 725
  development iterations and 12,249 action records collected with fixed
  workflows. We examine how strategies emerge, change, or are removed,
  and how different parts of the workflow contribute to decisions over
  time.

## 2 Related Work

#### Agentic workflows organize steps by interface or role.

Workflow representations organize computational steps and their
connections. DSPy composes declarative model-call modules ([Khattab
et al., 2024](#bib.bib5)). SEW connects role-based agents whose tasks
are specified by prompts ([Liu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib7)). AFlow writes
model calls and operators as code ([Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib14)).
HyEvo combines language model and code nodes ([Xu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib11)). LLM-as-Code keeps control flow in code and calls
models only for reasoning ([Qi et al., 2026](#bib.bib9)). These designs
organize a workflow around its interfaces and roles. The situation that
each step serves stays implicit in this structure. Our workflows name
these situations as explicit conditions and attach a procedure to each
one.

#### Self-evolving agents generate or revise programs.

Agent improvement ranges from candidate search to targeted revision.
TRACE updates program components from execution traces and
feedback ([Cheng et al., 2024](#bib.bib2)). ADAS generates programs from
an archive of evaluated agents ([Hu et al., 2025](#bib.bib4)). LLEGO
guides tree crossover and mutation with semantic priors ([Liu et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib8)). EvoSkillRec evolves recommender architectures by
recombining validated skills and generating new ones ([Li et al.,
2026](#bib.bib6)). Co-$`\pi`$-tree revises problematic branches ([Zhang
et al., 2026](#bib.bib13)). Trace2Policy patches rules from grouped
errors ([Zha et al., 2026](#bib.bib12)). HexMachina refines policies
through simulation ([Belle et al., 2025](#bib.bib1)). These methods
generate or revise programs, and the situations each part handles remain
implicit. Our agent names these situations and revises their boundaries,
so a revision can split or merge the game situations that one subtask
handles.

## 3 Self-Evolving Agentic Workflows

Our method separates the workflow that makes decisions from the agent
that improves it. The workflow is executable code and remains fixed
during an interaction. After execution, the agent may revise that code
using the resulting records and task outcomes
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")).

### 3.1 Programmatic Workflow

At iteration $`k`$, workflow $`W_{k}`$ specifies a decision structure
with its parameters and solution procedures. Given input $`x_{t}`$ and
interaction history $`h_{t}`$, it returns an action $`a_{t}`$ and
execution trace $`\tau_{t}`$:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       (a_{t},\tau_{t})=W_{k}(x_{t},h_{t})
       ```                                  |     | (1) |

The program may use conditions, function calls, nesting, and loops, so
its structure is not restricted to a decision tree
(Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Structure of the Final Workflows ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")).
Each operation can execute code directly or invoke a model. A model
operation may use an LLM for unresolved language-dependent decisions or
a learned predictor for an estimated quantity. The surrounding program
determines when an operation is used, supplies its inputs, and processes
its output. Model inference occurs only where specified by the workflow.

### 3.2 Workflow Evolution

At iteration $`k`$, the agent executes $`W_{k}`$ and collects execution
traces and task outcomes $`D_{k}`$. It examines poorly handled cases to
find problems in task decomposition, parameters or solution procedures.
It then constructs a candidate workflow from $`W_{k}`$ and $`D_{k}`$

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \widetilde{W}_{k+1}=\mathcal{A}(W_{k},D_{k})
       ```                                           |     | (2) |

Here, $`\mathcal{A}`$ selects revisions according to the diagnosed
problem. _(1) Task decomposition:_ split subtasks through observable
conditions or reorganize branches when distinct cases require different
decisions. _(2) Parameter adjustment:_ tune thresholds, weights, or
other numerical settings within an otherwise suitable procedure. _(3)
Model fitting:_ train or update classification or regression models from
execution data to estimate acceptance probabilities or continuation
values. _(4) Procedure redesign:_ devise an alternative strategy and
implement it through code or model reasoning when the current solution
is inadequate. The agent may combine these operations within an
iteration or reconsider earlier choices as further execution provides
new evidence.

The candidate is evaluated using replay, held-out records, or bounded
deployment to assess the targeted behavior and check for regressions
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Workflow Revisions by the Coding Agent ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")).
If retained, it becomes $`W_{k+1}`$; otherwise, $`W_{k+1}=W_{k}`$. The
next iteration executes the retained workflow and collects new feedback.
Revisions occur between interactions, while the workflow remains fixed
during each interaction.

## 4 Experiments

We evaluate competition performance (RQ1), workflow evolution (RQ2) and
agent behavior (RQ3).

### 4.1 Experimental Settings

We evaluate our agent on Bargaining, Negotiation and Persuasion in GLEE
against the other competition agents under the competition rules
(Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Compliance with GLEE Rules ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")).
Performance is the official GLEE rating, and efficiency is the local
decision time per action. GPT-5.5 revises the workflows from execution
feedback via our OpenProgram framework¹¹ 1
[https://github.com/fzkuji-neo/OpenProgram](https://github.com/fzkuji-neo/OpenProgram),
and Grok-4.6 serves the optional runtime LLM modules. Workflows stay
fixed within a game.
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Logs and Commit Histories ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")
describes the logs and commit histories.

### 4.2 Competition Results (RQ1)

This section presents the overall performance of the final workflows.
Our agent ranks first in the GLEE competition, and its ratings in all
three environments rise as the workflows evolve
(Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Competition Results (RQ1) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks"),
Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.3 Workflow Evolution (RQ2) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")).
In all three environments, the final workflows make each decision
locally within a millisecond.
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Competition Results ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")
gives the results, samples and strategies of each game.

| Mean branches per strategy node    | 2.13       | 2.25        | 2.24       |

### 4.3 Workflow Evolution (RQ2)

The agent keeps revising the workflow strategies throughout development.
The 26 representative strategy changes in
Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.3 Workflow Evolution (RQ2) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")
span iterations 12 to 689, and four of them come after iteration 600.
Revisions withdraw strategies as well as add them
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Workflow Revisions by the Coding Agent ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")).
A model judge enters Bargaining at iteration 40 and is disabled at 186.
The plateau exit enters at 552 and is withdrawn at 564, while a separate
Bargaining responder policy returns to shadow mode at iteration 557.

Each environment follows its own path, since every revision answers the
records of its own games. Negotiation first separates roles and hidden
types at iteration 12. It later probes the acceptance interval (415) and
mirrors seller concessions (462). It also remembers opponents across
games (468). Persuasion switches its signals at 31 and 62 and sells a
low-quality product after trust is built (612). Bargaining protects its
payoff at 285 and mirrors revealed demands at 313. The initial workflows
contain none of these procedures, which the agent derives from game
records.

Ratings move while the workflows change, and the shared axis places each
change against them. All three environments rise together around
iterations 236–244. The figure shows continuous revision. It does not
isolate the effect of any single change on the rating.

The competition rating rewards only a player’s own payoff. It ranks this
payoff among players in the same configuration and role, adjusted only
for the opponent’s rating. Neither the opponent’s payoff nor the joint
payoff enters the rating, and a deal that enlarges the total earns no
extra credit. Our evolved workflows become firm in asking and rejecting.
The final Bargaining workflow opens at a 55% self-share in all 63
eligible states. Its reservation lock rejects in 382 states. From
iteration 285 it also rejects non-final offers that leave it at most
10%.

Figure 2: Competition rating history and strategy changes on the same
725-iteration axis. Top: recorded deployment segments, one rating per
plotted iteration. Bottom: representative strategy changes, with
iteration numbers and operation markers.

### 4.4 Agent Behavior Analysis (RQ3)

Our agent decides through three kinds of modules, namely code, fitted
machine-learning models and LLM calls. Code makes up most of the
designed modules throughout development
(Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.4 Agent Behavior Analysis (RQ3) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")a).
Fitted models join as the workflows learn from recorded games, and LLM
modules remain as optional interfaces. These shares count designed
modules rather than decisions
(Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Hybrid Decision Making ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")).
Recorded actions follow the coded conditions, as with the opening rule
in every eligible Bargaining state.

Code and fitted models decide in under a millisecond, and the measured
LLM calls take seconds and mostly fail
(Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.4 Agent Behavior Analysis (RQ3) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")b).
Decision time depends on the executor and hardly on the number of
strategy judgments. The fast executors let the agent make every decision
locally within its turn.

In actual play, the LLM judge decides rarely and less over time
(Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.4 Agent Behavior Analysis (RQ3) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")).
Early on it answers about one in eleven non-message actions, almost all
of them Persuasion buyer decisions. Its answers agree with the code in
all but one case. The agent then makes these decisions deterministic,
and judge responses almost vanish after iteration 90. Code makes nearly
all final decisions from then on.

## 5 Conclusion

We present self-evolving agentic workflows that decompose tasks into
executable subtasks and revise their procedures from interaction
feedback. The GLEE study documents structural and procedural revisions,
with submillisecond mean local decision times. Controlled comparisons
are needed to quantify performance gains and costs across workflow
construction, execution, and revision.

## Appendix A Structure of the Final Workflows

This section shows what the final workflows look like. It gives the
order in which the code reaches one move and the procedures at each
game’s leaves. It then reports which branches the recorded states
actually reach.

### A.1 Execution Order for One Move

The final code reaches each move through three levels, and each level
answers a different question
(Figure [5](#A1.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ A.1 Execution Order for One Move ‣ Appendix A Structure of the Final Workflows ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")).
After the game is identified, ordered rules first name the current
situation. A second step reads further features and selects a procedure
for that situation. A last step turns the procedure into a concrete
offer or decision. The second level differs across games because their
main uncertainty differs. Bargaining reads the opponent’s concession
style from past offers. Negotiation first reads the type of our own
hidden value, which decides whether a profitable deal can exist.
Persuasion separates the seller and buyer roles and then tracks how
credible the seller’s signals have been. Keeping these questions on
separate levels lets a revision change one node while its siblings keep
their behavior, as the revision protocol in
Appendix [B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Revision Protocol ‣ Appendix B Workflow Revisions by the Coding Agent ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")
requires. All numbers come from code. The optional model calls at the
end can only choose among precomputed legal options or write message
text, which is consistent with the rare model decisions in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Hybrid Decision Making ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks").

Figure 5: Execution order of the final workflows for one move. Within a
box, rows are checked from top to bottom and indentation marks nested
checks; dashed boxes are optional model calls.

### A.2 Leaf Procedures by Game

In Bargaining, regime, opponent style, inflation, horizon, and
information select a named plan. Offer turns may use an evidence-gated
fitted offer before legal construction; response turns apply safety
rules, planned-continuation comparisons, fitted and trajectory models,
risk vetoes, and procedure-specific fallbacks in precedence order. In
Negotiation, the workflow computes own profit before opponent inference,
separates complete from incomplete information and open from finite
horizons, and applies ZOPA, Faratin/Boulware, take-profit, probe,
reservation, or walk procedures. In Persuasion, signals and
recommendation history update buyer belief and seller credibility;
leaves implement expected-value tests and recommendation rules.

### A.3 Bargaining Offer Model

The Bargaining offer fit standardizes share, progress, both visible
discounts, rejection count, last opponent share, and role. A logistic
model estimates acceptance and a ridge model estimates payoff after
rejection; the leaf maximizes discounted expected value over 35–60%
shares plus the rule fallback. Training requires minimum effective
sample sizes, chronological holdout improvement over a constant
baseline, and a negative share coefficient for acceptance. Runtime
replacement additionally requires an estimated edge above .015. The
current serialized accept and continuation tables have no shared
segment, so offer fitting returns the rule fallback. Response fitting
instead learns segment-specific acceptance margins under train, holdout,
and external replay gates. Serialized weights are loaded once per
process and remain fixed during a deployment.

### A.4 Branch Usage on Replayed States

A tree with many branches helps only if its branches handle real states,
so we also check where decisions go. We replay the decision states
recorded during development through the final revision. For each state,
we log its situation, its second-level split, and the procedure it
reaches
(Figure [6](#A1.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ A.4 Branch Usage on Replayed States ‣ Appendix A Structure of the Final Workflows ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")).
In Bargaining and Negotiation, two situations receive most states; in
Persuasion, the seller who observes product quality receives about half.
Within a situation, one or two procedures handle most states. The second
level matters most in the large situations: the patient Bargaining
situation, for instance, meets every opponent style. Rare situations,
such as the last round or one-round games, still keep their own leaves,
which were added for edge cases met during development. The second-level
splits also show how the workflows read their opponents. In about a
third of Persuasion buyer states, the seller is classified as lying.
These states mostly value the product by its expected value under a
lemons prior. Bargaining meets stubborn and mixed concession styles most
often.

Figure 6: Situations and procedures of the final workflows on replayed
decision states. Each row is one situation; its bar gives the share of
states, colored by the second-level split, and the right column lists
the procedures chosen within that situation.

These shares come from replayed development states rather than a new
tournament, so they reflect the opponents met during development. They
also show only which path the code takes. They do not measure how much
each branch adds to the rating or whether its decisions are optimal.

### A.5 Visited Decision Units

We deduplicate final selection node IDs in the Bargaining action traces
and final procedure names in Negotiation and Persuasion. This yields 58,
15, and 16 observed units, respectively. The inventory counts only
visited final-decision units, not all program branches, intermediate
computations, or dormant LLM call sites. Under the existing
final-executor taxonomy, Bargaining has 53 code units, one predictor
unit, and four unclassified units. Negotiation has 14 code units and one
procedure whose nine fitted-eligible actions do not reveal whether the
predictor displaced its numerical fallback. Persuasion has 16 code
units. Code combines rule and numerical labels; it does not imply that
no model was used in an upstream calculation. Runtime LLM judging is
disabled in these samples. The exported inventory records each unit’s
identifier, category, and action count; node cardinalities and execution
frequencies therefore remain distinct quantities.

## Appendix B Workflow Revisions by the Coding Agent

This section follows the coding agent as it revises the workflows. It
gives the protocol each revision follows and then inspects selected
revisions in detail. It ends with the revision activity across all 725
iterations.

### B.1 Revision Protocol

The recurring protocol reconstructed from repository instructions uses a
shared history-inspector prompt followed by a strategy prompt and one
family-specific routing prompt. The coding agent is instructed to open
the exact replay, reconstruct decision-time state, compute payoffs or
continuation values with diagnostic code, record the visited route,
modify only the affected node, preserve sibling behavior and the parent
fallback, and add a named replay. A revision names the target node,
semantic distinction, executor, fallback, and validation condition; the
coding agent commits the tree. The repository retains these instructions
and accepted code, but not one fixed design-time model identifier or a
complete proposal ledger.

### B.2 Inspected Revisions

We inventory the changed files and functions in all 725 commits of the
shared index; 530 touch the strategy-code paths considered in this
inventory. We then inspect 31 family-specific changes in detail and
display 26 selected events: ten in Bargaining, nine in Negotiation, and
seven in Persuasion. These are evidence-backed examples, not an
exhaustive classification or an estimate of how frequently each
operation occurs. A commit may contain several changes; its marker
identifies the specific mechanism inspected.

The mechanisms differ across environments. Negotiation introduces
acceptance-boundary search, concession mirroring, and persistent
opponent profiles. Persuasion instead changes which signal to send,
rotates rejected message templates, and uses established trust to
attempt low-quality sales. Its late buyer revision also separates two
operations: updating a posterior from the current opponent’s revealed
outcomes and refitting prior parameters from completed games. These
should not be combined into a generic adaptation category. Bargaining
includes a different sequence in which candidate policies gain and
subsequently lose decision authority.

Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.3 Workflow Evolution (RQ2) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")
compares selected revisions across environments. Both panels use a
single index constructed by merging the recorded main-branch,
family-lineage, and additional deployment commits, deduplicating hashes,
and ordering commits by timestamp, with hash order breaking ties. Each
deployment rating and strategy marker is mapped by its commit hash, so
their horizontal positions are directly comparable. The following case
studies retain the 359-commit main-branch positions used in the source
audit; these are distinct from the shared plotting index. The operation
categories describe recorded changes, not prescribed development stages.

### B.3 Selected Revision Cases

Bargaining already has discrete opponent categories in the earliest
snapshot; decomposition does not first appear at a later marked commit.
The subsequent history contains both more specific conditions and
consolidation of existing logic. At position 82, a unified planner
replaces several route-specific implementations. Positions 236–268 add
continuous opponent state and fitted continuation estimates with recency
weighting. We examine concrete revisions rather than treating
commit-message keywords as measurements of the agent’s reasoning.

#### From an opponent category to an observed state.

Position 236 adds an opponent-state estimator that records recent
concessions, repeated offers, and rejections of our offers. The
distinction affects execution: for a patient player facing an unknown
horizon, a repeatedly observed offer can justify ending the interaction
even below an earlier acceptance boundary.
Figure [7](#A2.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ From an opponent category to an observed state. ‣ B.3 Selected Revision Cases ‣ Appendix B Workflow Revisions by the Coding Agent ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")
reconstructs the added branch and its regression cases. Two existing
tests change their expected decision from rejection to acceptance. A new
test accepts a repeated $`45.2\%`$ self-share, while its $`48\%`$
variant still rejects. The change therefore implements a narrowly
defined response to a plateau rather than uniformly lowering every
threshold. Semantic refinement here changes which history features
determine a decision, not only the wording of a prompt.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 7: An actual Bargaining revision. Left: the acceptance branch
introduced at position 236, with all its conditions and the fallback to
the existing procedure. Right: the motivating situation and expected
behavior documented in the same commit’s tests. Earlier branches retain
precedence. The diagram shows a local code change, not the entire
workflow.

#### A proposed strategy need not remain in the workflow.

At position 289, a candidate counteroffer mirrors the share revealed by
the opponent. In its round-two, equal-discount branch, it requests a
self-share of $`\min(0.60,\max(0.55,1-s))`$, where $`s`$ is the share
offered to us. Position 291 removes this branch in a rollback explicitly
described as withdrawing unvalidated changes. This is evidence of
proposal and withdrawal, not proof that mirroring reduced scores. It
also differs from opening imitation in the fixed-workflow analysis: one
responds to the current opponent’s offer, whereas the other applies an
opening rule. Treating both as a single strategy label would conceal
their different conditions and retention histories.

#### Reconsidering which evidence controls a branch.

Position 284 removes an acceptance override triggered by phrases in the
opponent’s message, combined with specific share ranges. The removed
branch could accept because the message announced a final offer or
willingness to close. Removing it reduces the direct influence of
opponent-controlled wording on that decision. Together with the state
estimator, this illustrates a substantive change in policy design:
deciding which observations should justify an action, rather than only
adding more branches.

#### Changes outside Bargaining.

At position 2, Negotiation separates hidden strong types from cases
where a small positive gain remains acceptable; its final-round rule
still accepts a nonnegative gain. The commit records earlier cases that
conceded to reservation and then accepted a very small surplus.
Persuasion’s August 24 development record describes a different failure:
skipping an early low-quality recommendation can leave an otherwise
profitable buyer unwilling to buy later recommendations. The proposed
response recommends low-quality items until the first sale and changes
behavior thereafter. This dated inspector record supplies the
development rationale, whereas the Negotiation example is supported by a
versioned policy change and regression tests. These cases show why
identical revision categories do not imply identical strategies across
environments.

### B.4 Bargaining Milestones

The retained Bargaining history begins with discrete semantic routing
and dormant after-game adaptation. It subsequently adds anti-gifting
defense at position 22, broad bounded judging at 40, ambiguity-only
judging at 55, and a unified plan pipeline at 82. Bargaining judging is
disabled at 186. Positions 236–268 enrich opponent state and add
evidence-gated fitting, continuation modeling, bounded predictions, and
recency weighting. Later changes emphasize validation: a lowball
response is removed at 271, rating-risk defense appears at 281, audit
instrumentation appears at 283, text-controlled routing is removed at
284, the mirroring candidate is removed at 291, and a broader response
family is rolled back at 294. Position 315 introduces replay-first
branch ordering. These are selected code milestones, not a complete
deployment history or estimates of individual rating effects.

### B.5 Function Edit Inventory

The separate source audit uses the 725 revisions in the shared commit
index. For each revision, we compare Python function definitions in the
three environment-specific workflow directories with the same files in
its first parent. We count module-level functions and class methods;
nested local functions remain part of their enclosing function. A
definition is identified by its file path and qualified name. Additions
and removals change this inventory; modifications change the abstract
syntax tree of an existing definition. Formatting and comments do not
count as modifications, whereas changed docstrings do. Renaming or
moving a function counts as a removal and an addition. Shared workflow
utilities, external model wrappers, and tests are outside this
inventory. Function counts therefore measure the inspected code
structure, not the number of decision nodes or model calls.

The archived source-audit data sum these edit instances across
environments in trailing 50-position windows before computing
proportions. A window without edits is missing rather than zero. Each
version is compared with its own first parent, not with the preceding
snapshot in the cross-branch plotting order. Cherry-picked changes on
different branches remain separate edit instances. The function-count
series includes only the 359 main-branch snapshots, mapped onto the same
shared index, so lines do not connect unrelated branch states. These
statistics neither identify the author of an edit nor attribute a
performance gain to it.

### B.6 Revision Activity across All Iterations

The main text and the cases above show selected revisions. This
subsection follows revision work across all 725 iterations. It asks
where the code changes and which revision operation each change applies.
It also asks how the coding agent justifies, undoes and checks its
changes.

#### Labeling revision operations.

We compare each iteration with its first parent at the level of
functions, methods and module constants in the workflow code. Each
changed unit receives one of the four revision operations of our method.
A change that disappears once numeric constants are masked is a
parameter adjustment. A change to the condition of an if, elif or while
statement is task decomposition, since it changes when a subtask
applies. Any other change to a function body is procedure redesign.
Added or removed functions count as decomposition in classification and
routing files and as redesign elsewhere. Changed learned artifacts and
fitting code count as model fitting. Function edits follow the source
audit above.

#### Where the code changes.

Revision work moves from the main line to experimental branches and back
(Figure [8](#A2.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Where the code changes. ‣ B.6 Revision Activity across All Iterations ‣ Appendix B Workflow Revisions by the Coding Agent ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")a).
The first 258 iterations all lie on the main line. From iteration 259
onward, most work happens on experimental branches, and selected changes
later return to the main line. Edits arrive in two large bursts
(Figure [8](#A2.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Where the code changes. ‣ B.6 Revision Activity across All Iterations ‣ Appendix B Workflow Revisions by the Coding Agent ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")b).
The first iteration builds the initial workflow. Iterations 486–496
restructure Negotiation: one commit splits its tactics into separate
modules, and another refactors them without a policy change. Between
these bursts, most edits modify existing functions. Task decomposition
appears in nearly every interval, while procedure redesign comes in
bursts
(Figure [8](#A2.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Where the code changes. ‣ B.6 Revision Activity across All Iterations ‣ Appendix B Workflow Revisions by the Coding Agent ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")c).
Decomposition changes 738 units in 458 commits, and redesign changes 591
units in 188 commits. Parameter adjustment and model fitting each change
fewer than 35 units. Most revision work thus sharpens the conditions of
existing subtasks.

Figure 8: Revision activity per 25 iterations. (a) Commits on the main
line and on experimental branches. (b) Added, modified and removed
workflow functions. (c) Changed code units by revision operation.

#### Different games in different periods.

Each game is revised in its own period
(Figure [9](#A2.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Different games in different periods. ‣ B.6 Revision Activity across All Iterations ‣ Appendix B Workflow Revisions by the Coding Agent ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")).
Bargaining changes throughout development. Negotiation work grows
between iterations 300 and 550 and contains the restructuring burst.
Persuasion changes in the first 250 iterations and again after iteration 580. Model fitting first appears at iterations 240–243, inside the
interval where all three ratings rise in the main text. This timing does
not show that fitting causes the rise.

Figure 9: Changed code units per 25 iterations by game and revision
operation. Shared modules hold code and learned artifacts used by more
than one game.

#### How the coding agent justifies and undoes changes.

The coding agent changes how it argues for a revision
(Figure [10](#A2.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ How the coding agent justifies and undoes changes. ‣ B.6 Revision Activity across All Iterations ‣ Appendix B Workflow Revisions by the Coding Agent ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")).
In the first 50 iterations, many commit messages cite a specific game
and patch the case it reveals. One message records a game that rejected
a 44% share in round one and accepted the same share in round seven. The
next workflow accepts 43% or more through round six. Such citations then
nearly vanish, and only a few later Negotiation fixes cite games again.
Later messages name a validation step, such as a replay or a shadow run.
These mentions peak near iterations 250 and 550. Thirteen commits
restore an earlier strategy policy, and most of them come after
iteration 300.

Figure 10: Evidence named in commit messages across iterations. Curves
give the smoothed share of iterations with each mark. Ticks below mark
the individual commits.

Some policies change direction several times before they settle
(Table [2](#A2.T2 "Table 2 ‣ How the coding agent justifies and undoes changes. ‣ B.6 Revision Activity across All Iterations ‣ Appendix B Workflow Revisions by the Coding Agent ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")).
The Persuasion seller first skips a low-quality product, then recommends
it and then skips it again. At iteration 31 the agent ends this swing
with a new condition. The seller recommends low-quality products until
the first sale and changes behavior after it. The disagreement is thus
resolved by decomposition. A Bargaining plateau exit runs in shadow
mode, goes live, is reverted and returns with a guard. It is then split
by horizon type. A Rubinstein responder is promoted and demoted twice
within eight iterations. Evolution therefore includes trial, withdrawal
and repair besides steady growth.

| Policy                                       | Steps                                                                                                                                                          |
| -------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Persuasion seller with a low-quality product | 1 skip $`\rightarrow`$ 22 recommend $`\rightarrow`$ 29 skip $`\rightarrow`$ 31 recommend until the first sale                                                  |
| Bargaining plateau exit                      | 548 shadow $`\rightarrow`$ 552 live $`\rightarrow`$ 564 reverted $`\rightarrow`$ 579 live with a guard $`\rightarrow`$ 585 split into finite and open horizons |
| Bargaining Rubinstein responder              | 553 shadow $`\rightarrow`$ 556 live $`\rightarrow`$ 557 shadow $`\rightarrow`$ 559 live on a narrower band $`\rightarrow`$ 560 shadow                          |

Table 2: Policies that change direction during development. Each step
gives the iteration and the behavior that follows it.

#### How changes are checked.

Revisions carry regression tests
(Figure [11](#A2.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ How changes are checked. ‣ B.6 Revision Activity across All Iterations ‣ Appendix B Workflow Revisions by the Coding Agent ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")).
Test functions on the main line grow from 165 to 595. Of the 527 commits
that change strategy code, 493 also change tests. The share drops only
around the restructuring burst. Each test fixes a diagnosed problem as
an expected decision
(Table [3](#A2.T3 "Table 3 ‣ How changes are checked. ‣ B.6 Revision Activity across All Iterations ‣ Appendix B Workflow Revisions by the Coding Agent ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")).
Later revisions can then change one branch and still detect changes in
the others.

Figure 11: Regression tests during development. (a) Test functions on
the main line. (b) Share of strategy commits per 25 iterations that also
change tests.

| Iteration | Problem                               | Revision                                   | Test checks that                                                   |
| --------- | ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| 97        | Message wording misread               | Refine conditions                          | a current recommendation outweighs earlier skip wording            |
| 110       | Opponent style misjudged              | Update the estimate                        | recent stalls, not an early concession, set the style              |
| 285       | Low-payoff deals accepted             | Refine conditions                          | a non-final offer at the bottom of the field is not accepted       |
| 608       | Same message rejected again and again | Refine conditions and change the procedure | a rejected counter message is not sent again                       |
| 676       | Opponent misjudged                    | Update the estimate and refine conditions  | the current opponent’s revealed outcomes override the global prior |

Table 3: Diagnosed problems, the revisions they trigger and the
regression tests that record them.

#### Limits.

The operation labels come from syntactic rules. A changed condition may
fix a bug without splitting a subtask, and a mixed change counts once
for each operation it contains. The counts measure code change and not
its effect on the rating. Not every experimental branch was deployed.
Commit messages show how the agent describes a change. They do not prove
that the described validation ran.

### C.1 Large Rating Changes

The recorded interval ending at position 243 contains increases of
107.16 rating points over 267 Bargaining games, 147.19 over 262
Negotiation games, and 139.64 over 267 Persuasion games. Thus, the
visible increase is not confined to the Bargaining branch annotated on
the curve. The extended history captures later changes: the Bargaining
rating rises from 2331.96 to 2631.70 at the same recorded revision, then
reaches 2760.27 at a subsequent deployment. Negotiation declines from
2923.32 to 1844.08 before recovering. These are changes between rating
observations, not single-match effects or controlled estimates of a code
edit.
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Workflow Revisions by the Coding Agent ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")
therefore examines the implementation and behavior records to explain
what changed in the strategy itself.

## Appendix D Hybrid Decision Making

The agent decides through code, fitted models and LLM calls; this
section measures how much of the play each one decides. It first counts
decision points in the source code and then attributes recorded actions
to executors. It ends with how often the LLM is called and what that use
is associated with.

### D.1 Decision Sites in the Source Code

The module shares in
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.4 Agent Behavior Analysis (RQ3) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")
come solely from committed source code. They do not use action logs or
infer an executor from missing log entries. We inspect the three
environment-specific workflow directories at each of the 359 main-branch
revisions. A code site is one syntactic conditional statement,
conditional expression, while-condition, or match selector. Compound
Boolean tests count as one site rather than one site per comparison. The
inventory includes intermediate routing and eligibility checks as well
as final-action checks; it is not restricted to leaves.

An ML site is an explicit call to the fitted prediction interfaces,
segmented prediction interfaces, learned-policy lookup, or
rating-surrogate prediction interface. Imported aliases are resolved
before classification. Model-internal arithmetic and coefficient-loading
routines are not counted again. The shared LLM candidate-selection
interface contributes one site per environment where the player calls
the judge and the source does not unconditionally reject that
environment. Runtime configuration may disable this interface; its
presence does not imply an actual invocation. Message generation and the
agent’s workflow-editing calls are outside this decision-site inventory.

We sum site counts across the three environments and divide each
executor count by their sum. These percentages partition the defined
sites, not executed actions. Source definitions can contain dormant
functions or guarded paths; this inventory does not prove path
feasibility. Counts depend on the chosen syntactic granularity, so a
model interface and its internal calculations must not be interpreted as
equal computational work. File paths, blob hashes, line numbers,
expressions, and revision-to-source mappings accompany the exported
counts. There is no smoothing or interpolation between sampled
revisions; the curves use steps.

### D.2 Executor Attribution of Actions

The separate runtime-attribution analysis counts executed non-message
actions, not functions, distinct code branches, or construction-time
agent calls. An LLM label denotes a persisted valid candidate selection,
including selections that retain the original action. Code combines the
audited rule and numerical procedures. An ML-model label denotes an
identified fitted-model decision. Records without sufficient evidence
remain unclassified and stay in the denominator. These runtime
statistics are not the source of
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.4 Agent Behavior Analysis (RQ3) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks").

The historical panel reuses the 57,179 replay actions and 233
valid-selection records described below. The remainder is unclassified
because the replay export lacks exhaustive executor labels; a zero
confirmed count for code or ML does not establish zero use. The trailing
window spans ten main-branch commit positions, with numerator and
denominator summed before normalization. Positions are mapped onto the
shared commit index, and intervals without recorded actions are missing
rather than zero. This panel therefore shows attribution coverage and
confirmed decisions, not a complete three-executor transition.

The fixed-version panel excludes 1,957 seller-message records from the
12,249-row sample, leaving 10,292 non-message actions. Bargaining
contains 2,305 code decisions, eight identified predictor decisions, and
31 unresolved decisions. Negotiation contains 1,903 code decisions and
nine unresolved decisions for which a fitted candidate is recorded but
its selection over the numerical fallback is not identifiable. All 6,036
non-message Persuasion actions use the audited code procedures. Runtime
LLM selection is disabled in these three samples. Their observed
executor shares are not extrapolated to earlier versions, and the
Persuasion sample is not assigned a historical commit because its loaded
runtime hash is unknown.

### D.3 Condition-to-Action Checks

We test alignment with the implemented policy by checking branch
conditions against recorded actions. During development, regression
tests accompany nearly every strategy revision
(Appendix [B.6](#A2.SS6 "B.6 Revision Activity across All Iterations ‣ Appendix B Workflow Revisions by the Coding Agent ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")).
In the fixed Bargaining batch, opening imitation selects a $`55\%`$
self-share in all 63 eligible states. The reservation condition applies
to 451 states, but its rejection procedure handles only 382: the
remaining 69 take higher-precedence branches, producing 57 rejections
and 12 acceptances. The low-share predictor condition activates eight
times, all followed by rejection
(Table [5](#A4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ D.3 Condition-to-Action Checks ‣ Appendix D Hybrid Decision Making ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")).

| Condition                | Eligible | Executed | Recorded action            |
| ------------------------ | -------- | -------- | -------------------------- |
| Opening imitation        | 63       | 63       | offer $`55\%`$ self-share  |
| Reservation lock         | 451      | 382      | reject below $`60\%/47\%`$ |
| Low-share predictor gate | 8        | 8        | reject                     |

Table 5: Condition-to-action checks on fixed Bargaining records.
Eligibility does not imply execution when an earlier condition takes
precedence.

The inventory contains 512 Bargaining games with 2,344 action rows, 199
Negotiation games with 1,912 rows, and 401 Persuasion games with 7,993
rows. Every trace matches the target agent, assigned batch, game family,
and deployment identifier. All three deployments set freeze_policy=true,
llm_judge=false, and llm_messages=false. The batch outcome ledgers are
partial or contaminated, so we use their action traces but not batch
rating deltas.

The exporter checks Bargaining routes directly from persisted state,
actions, and named selection nodes. It finds 63 states eligible for the
field-imitation opening, all 63 routed to the node, spanning 60 games
with no action violation. The raw patient-reservation predicate holds
for 451 states: 382 route to the reservation lock, while 69 take
higher-priority veto or exit branches. The reservation activations span
83 games and have no branch violation. The severe-low-share predictor
gate appears eight times in six games, and all eight actions reject. A
separate legality pass finds zero schema or offer-budget violations
among all 2,344 Bargaining action rows from 512 games. These checks
establish behavior on logged states, not counterfactual route coverage
or the accuracy of every upstream semantic classification.

### D.4 Executor Labels in Frozen Deployments

The checked conditions match recorded behavior, and all 2,344 Bargaining
actions satisfy schema and budget constraints; this does not establish
decision optimality. The fixed batches contain 512 Bargaining, 199
Negotiation, and 401 Persuasion games.
Figure [12](#A4.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ D.4 Executor Labels in Frozen Deployments ‣ Appendix D Hybrid Decision Making ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")
shows their recorded decision labels. Bargaining has 2,022 rule-labeled
actions, 283 numerical actions, eight predictor actions, and 31
unclassified actions. Negotiation has 16 rule-labeled actions,
1,887–1,896 numerical actions, and up to nine predictor actions; those
nine records do not identify whether the fitted candidate displaced its
fallback. Persuasion has 4,987 rule-labeled and 3,006 numerical actions.
These labels identify the final recorded procedure, not every
computation performed earlier in the workflow. Their definitions differ
across environments, preventing direct comparison as a common measure of
model dependence.

For Bargaining, the severe-low-share fitted node is a predictor;
trajectory, model, strict-dominance, and risk stages are numeric; and
legacy semantic stages are rules. This yields 2,022 rule, 283 numeric,
and 8 predictor rows, while 31 rows in four newer stages remain
unclassified. For Negotiation, walk is a rule and other named procedures
are numeric by default. Nine faratin_boulware rows expose paired fitted
scores but do not record whether a fitted proposal displaced its numeric
fallback, producing only loose bounds of 16 rule, 1,887–1,896 numeric,
and 0–9 predictor rows. Persuasion’s expected-value procedures are
numeric and its trust-, history-, or threshold-conditioned procedures
are rules; source inspection classifies three learned_low_text rows as
rules, producing 4,987 rule and 3,006 numeric rows. These categories
describe final recorded selection nodes, not every upstream computation.
The family mappings are not equivalent: Bargaining uses final-node/stage
labels, whereas Negotiation and Persuasion use named-procedure
taxonomies. Persuasion also lacks a runtime commit, so its action
evidence is deployment-specific but not commit-aligned.

### D.5 LLM Judge Usage

A bounded judge appears at position 40, is restricted to ambiguous cases

while action-changing picks account for $`0.081\%`$ and $`0.015\%`$ of
recorded actions. The later window contains fewer observed interventions
relative to its action count, but coverage differs between windows.
Failed or unrecognized invocations are missing, precluding a total
inference-cost estimate.

### D.6 Runtime Parameters and Timing

Runtime LLM calls use temperature 0.2 and a 120-token output limit.
Decision times average ten replays of each logged state with warmed
code. Workflow statistics in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Competition Results (RQ1) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")
count named classifiers as multiway nodes and exclude technical checks.
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.4 Agent Behavior Analysis (RQ3) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")a
smooths module shares over 11 iterations.
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.4 Agent Behavior Analysis (RQ3) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")b
times 1,420 code and 450 regression attempts and five LLM calls. Two LLM
calls return valid responses and three fail.
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Competition Results (RQ1) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")
averages ten timings per state over 67, 60 and 60 offline states.

### D.7 Model Use and Rating Changes

The score panel uses disjoint 20-commit intervals beginning at position
72, with the last interval ending at 223. Within each family and
interval, we retain unique replay games with recorded non-message
actions and finite rating deltas. The rate numerator, action
denominator, and mean game-level rating change all use these same games.
The finite-rating subset contains 5,477 games and 57,097 actions; five
games with 82 action records are excluded because a finite rating delta
is unavailable. Each point is one family–interval group; groups need at
least ten games, and all 24 groups meet this threshold. No score shift
is attributed to individual model decisions: versions, opponents, and
game conditions differ, and no counterfactual execution was performed.
Model-log absence does not establish code execution. Historical turn
exports contain actions and outcomes but no exhaustive final-executor
labels, so they do not support a three-way LLM/code/predictor area
chart. The fixed-deployment taxonomy in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Competition Results (RQ1) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")
is not extrapolated to earlier commits.

## Appendix E Logs and Commit Histories

All counts in this paper come from deployment logs and the commit
histories of the game repository. This section lists these data and
explains how the commit counts relate. It then describes how episodes
are aligned with deployments and what cannot be released.

### E.1 Data Sources

We study three GLEE environments across 359 first-parent commits
(_commit positions_). We align 166 startup-rating records with 159
revisions, ending at position 256. Three fixed-workflow deployments
provide 1,112 games and 12,249 action records, including messages, with
runtime LLM judging disabled. Archived deployment logs extend the
performance history to 799 family-rating observations across 389
recorded revisions.
Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.3 Workflow Evolution (RQ2) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Agentic Workflowsvia Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks")
shows a segmented summary, retaining one observation per plotted
revision. Deployment hashes locate observations; they do not establish
which edit caused a rating change.

### E.2 Commit Indices

The paper uses two commit indices. The main branch’s first-parent path
has 359 commits. Its positions serve the deployment alignment and the
case studies. The shared index merges these commits with family-lineage
branches and additional deployment commits. It deduplicates hashes and
orders the 725 commits by timestamp. The figures and the source audit
use this index. Of its 725 commits, 530 touch strategy code.

### E.3 Episode-to-Deployment Alignment

We enumerate 359 commits on the main branch’s first-parent path. Each
episode is assigned to the latest target-agent deployment whose
timestamp does not exceed its start time, and that revision is mapped to
a first-parent position. Judge logs begin carrying game IDs at position 71. Positions 72–89 include 330 episodes, of which 301 have 2,468
recorded non-message actions; positions 90–223 include 5,672 episodes,
of which 5,181 have 54,711. The turn export skips 25,216 empty or
message-only actions. We count a valid pick when a matched judge outcome
exists and an action-changing pick only when that event replaces the
deterministic candidate. Failed, timed-out, cooldown, or unrecognized
picks return before this event and usually lack a game ID, so invocation
totals cannot be aligned to deployment windows. The pre-Git agent log
records 586 direct-LLM actions but lacks a turn denominator and commit
mapping.

The deployment mapping ends at commit position 256. Positions 257–315
are checked-in code milestones without a retained target-deployment
assignment, and the verified September 1 rating endpoint is likewise
commit-unassigned.

### E.4 Release Limits

The local research package contains exporter scripts and the derived
CSV/JSON used for the figures. It is not yet a public reproduction
artifact: raw interaction logs cannot be redistributed, and the exporter
contains local deployment identifiers. Without those logs, the
historical export cannot be regenerated end to end.

## Appendix F Compliance with GLEE Rules

GLEE permits hand-coded heuristics and agent-code updates. The workflow
uses only API-provided game state, visible history, and legal-action
metadata. It does not automate the Human Track, select actions through
live human intervention, coordinate accounts, or exploit undocumented
game behavior.
